claim: MTDSim is an existing MTD simulator, from Brown et al.
quote: This paper proposes an evaluation framework named MTDSim, which is a simulation-based tool to evaluate the effectiveness of combinations of MTD techniques against practical and realistic attack scenarios.
issue: Brown proposes MTDSim as a simulation-based evaluation tool; 'as the APT attacker model' is the dissertation's own use.

claim: MTDSim simulates an attacker and MTD on one network
quote: We develop an MTD evaluation framework named MTDSim, which will be used to simulate the system, attacker, and defense.
issue: 'system, attacker, and defense'; the network is one generated HARM held identical across scenarios (Sec. IV, p. 5).

claim: MTDSim evaluates MTD mechanisms singly and in combination
quote: When a single MTD was used, the host shuffle performed the best, followed by port shuffling.
issue: Brown runs single, double and triple MTD (Fig. 4a-c); the purpose statement (p. 1) names combinations.

claim: Each deeper level is a set of subnets
quote: the graphs are generated using the Barabasi-Albert graph model [16] to generate small subnets in each level of depth, which mimics the characteristics of real-world networks. ... Internal hosts will also be displayed if they are able to establish a path through a compromised or exposed internal host.
locator: p. 2 printed (PDF p. 2), Sec. III-A; Sec. III-C(2), p. 4
issue: 'small subnets in each level of depth'.

claim: Subnets are small groups of densely linked hosts, each level joined to the level before it, so reaching a level requires a compromised host in the level before it
quote: the graphs are generated using the Barabasi-Albert graph model [16] to generate small subnets in each level of depth, which mimics the characteristics of real-world networks. ... Internal hosts will also be displayed if they are able to establish a path through a compromised or exposed internal host.
locator: p. 2 printed (PDF p. 2), Sec. III-A; Sec. III-C(2), p. 4
issue: Brown says small Barabasi-Albert subnets per level and that internal hosts become visible through a path from a compromised or exposed host; it never says 'densely linked', that each level joins only the level before, or that reaching a level requires a compromised host in the previous level (Fig. 2 draws the levels but the text states no such rule). The strict level-by-level rule is the code's.
fix_text: add the code source for the level-joining rule, e.g. "... in the level before it \citep{brown2023, tay2024code}", or tighten "densely linked" to "small groups of linked hosts"

claim: Each vulnerability has an attack complexity derived from CVSS and an impact
quote: Vulnerabilities are generated with an attack complexity and impact, derived from the CVSS scoring system [23]. The attack complexity would decide the difficulty of exploiting the vulnerability, randomly generated between [0.4, 1] and the impact decides the reward for compromising the vulnerability, randomly generated between [0, 1].
locator: p. 3 printed (PDF p. 3), Sec. III-A, Vulnerability Layer

claim: Attack complexity sets the probability that an exploit succeeds; impact is the damage a successful exploit does
quote: Vulnerabilities are generated with an attack complexity and impact, derived from the CVSS scoring system [23]. The attack complexity would decide the difficulty of exploiting the vulnerability, randomly generated between [0.4, 1] and the impact decides the reward for compromising the vulnerability, randomly generated between [0, 1].
locator: p. 3 printed (PDF p. 3), Sec. III-A, Vulnerability Layer
issue: Brown: attack complexity 'would decide the difficulty of exploiting the vulnerability' (not a probability) and impact 'decides the reward for compromising the vulnerability' (the attacker's reward, not damage). The probability reading and 'damage' are the dissertation's (or the code's) interpretation; in MTDSim attack complexity also sets exploit time (U0121).
fix_text: "which sets the probability that an exploit succeeds" -> "which sets how hard an exploit is"; or keep and add the code source for the probability use

claim: The MTD mechanism pool originates with Brown and was added to by Zhang
quote: The following MTD techniques are implemented for evaluations, which cover various types of MTD techniques in multiple system layers.
locator: p. 3 printed (PDF p. 3), Sec. III-A, Vulnerability Layer, Sec. III-B(1)-(6)
issue: Brown implements six: IP, port, user access and host topology shuffles, service and OS diversity, which are six of the table's seven; complete topology shuffle is Zhang's.

claim: The baseline attacker is the attacker MTDSim was built with
quote: Attacker is modeled as a theoretically intelligent adversary, which will follow a logical flowchart inspired by the Cyber Kill Chain [17] and MITRE ATT&CK Framework [18].
locator: p. 2 printed (PDF p. 2), Sec. III; Sec. III-C, p. 4

claim: The attacker follows a fixed procedure modelled on the Cyber Kill Chain
quote: The adversaries are implemented to follow a process similar to the Cyber Kill Chain [17] and MITRE ATT&CK Framework [18] as depicted in Figure 3.
locator: p. 4 printed (PDF p. 4), Sec. III-C(2); Sec. V-A, p. 7
issue: Brown names the Cyber Kill Chain and MITRE ATT&CK; dropping ATT&CK narrows, not overstates. 'Fixed': 'will always follow the attack procedure' (p. 7).

claim: The procedure is six attack actions: scan for hosts, enumerate one, scan its ports, exploit, brute-force, scan the neighbours of each compromised host
quote: The attacker will commence with the host discovery phase. This encompasses performing a scan on the network to discover all exposed hosts. ... Host reconnaissance is performed next, running port scans to discover exposed services or internal services that are connected to the compromised service. ... Once the attacker has successfully compromised a host, they will assume command and control functionality, making it possible to view internal services and hosts that are connected to it. If the attack fails, they will then commence a brute force attack.
locator: p. 4 printed (PDF p. 4), Sec. III-C(2); Fig. 3, p. 5
issue: The five named steps are in Brown's prose; 'enumerate one' is Fig. 3 box 2 ('Pick a Target Host from Priority Stack'), scan neighbours is box 9. But Brown's Fig. 3 has ten boxes, including the credential-reuse check (box 4) as its own step; the count of six attack actions is MTDSim's code grouping, not Brown's.

claim: The baseline attacker has two attack scenarios, a general one (compromise as many hosts as possible) and a targeted one (compromise a target host)
quote: where the attacker is looking to obtain the most amount of control by attempting to compromise the whole network. ... In the Target Attack Scenario, like APT-style attacks, the attacker is looking to compromise a specific ”target” host (e.g., a credential database).
locator: p. 4 printed (PDF p. 4), Sec. III-C(1); Sec. IV-A, p. 5
issue: Goal wording of the general scenario also at p. 5: 'the attack goal is to compromise as many hosts as possible'.

claim: On each host the attacker tries stolen credentials first, then exploits vulnerabilities in order of return on attack, and brute force last
quote: The attacker will first attempt to perform a credential ... using user account information from previously compromised hosts. Next, a service from the scanning will be selected for exploitation. The vulnerabilities from all the services scanned will be put into a priority stack based on their return on attack (RoA) [13]. ... If the attack fails, they will then commence a brute force attack. If all attack options fail, they will then choose another host to exploit.
locator: p. 4 printed (PDF p. 4), Sec. III-C(2); Fig. 3, p. 5

claim: Return on attack is an exploit's probability of success times its impact, divided by the time it takes
quote: The vulnerabilities from all the services scanned will be put into a priority stack based on their return on attack (RoA) [13].
issue: Brown names RoA only as the priority key and cites its ref. [13] (Alavizadeh et al. 2018) for it; it gives no formula, and nothing about time as the denominator. The citation sits directly on the definition, so the definition is attributed to Brown. The time denominator is presumably MTDSim's code.
fix_text: move \citep{brown2023} to after "in order of \emph{return on attack}" and cite the definition to its source (e.g. \citep{cremonini2005, alavizadeh2022}, as Table 3.1 does for RoA, plus tay2024code if the time denominator is the code's)

quote: The attacker will first attempt to perform a credential ... using user account information from previously compromised hosts. issue: Uncited but Brown says it ('If all attack options fail, they will then choose another host to exploit'); the paragraph's citation at U0119 covers it.

quote: the attacker agent will move on after trying to exploit for 10 times without being able to compromise the host currently selected. However, when the attacker is conducting a targeted attack (i.e., scenario 2), the attacker is set to never give up on the target node.
locator: p. 7 printed (PDF p. 7), Sec. V-C; Table I, p. 5
issue: Table I: 'No. of atack attempts before giving up 10'.

claim: The attacker never gives up on a target host
quote: the attacker agent will move on after trying to exploit for 10 times without being able to compromise the host currently selected. However, when the attacker is conducting a targeted attack (i.e., scenario 2), the attacker is set to never give up on the target node.
issue: Brown scopes it to the targeted scenario, where target hosts exist; no condition dropped.

claim: A vulnerability's attack complexity lies between 0.4 and 1
quote: The attack complexity would decide the difficulty of exploiting the vulnerability, randomly generated between [0.4, 1]
locator: p. 3 printed (PDF p. 3), Sec. III-A, Vulnerability Layer; Table I, p. 5

claim: An exploit takes 15 s times one minus the vulnerability's attack complexity, so 0 to 9 s
quote: The attack complexity would decide the difficulty of exploiting the vulnerability, randomly generated between [0.4, 1]
locator: p. 3 printed (PDF p. 3), Sec. III-A, Vulnerability Layer
issue: Brown gives no exploit duration at all (its only time quantity is the defence trigger time, in ms). The citation sits after the range clause, but the sentence reads as attributing the 15 s formula to Brown too, and the formula then has no source; the tex comment says it was verified against services.py Vulnerability.exploit_time, i.e. the code.
fix_text: "An exploit takes 15\,s times one minus the vulnerability's attack complexity~\citep{tay2024code}, which lies between 0.4 and 1~\citep{brown2023}"

claim: (uncited neighbour) A host-layer deployment disrupts the attacker and sends it back to scanning hosts, because the host may have moved
quote: IP Shuffle and Host Topology Shuffle change the location of the host by changing the IP or the host itself. This would result in the attacker’s connection to the host being terminated or timed out. As they would be uncertain of the status of the hosts, they would be forced to re-perform the host discovery phase to find new paths to the hosts.
issue: Brown's IP and host topology shuffles force a return to host discovery. 'During any attack action' is close to Brown's 'interrupting any attacker performing operations using an incorrect IP Address' (p. 3). Uncited; the U0124 citation follows in the next sentence and plausibly covers both.

claim: A service-layer deployment disrupts the attacker only while it scans ports, exploits or brute-forces
quote: Service and Operating System Diversity, and Port Shuffle all change the services on the host. This would either change the ports that the services are run on or change the service itself, changing the vulnerabilities. This would block the attacker from compromising the vulnerability and force them to re-perform a port scan to understand the new service or the service location.
issue: Brown says the service-changing mechanisms 'block the attacker from compromising the vulnerability' (exploit); it does not name port scanning or brute force, nor say 'only'. The three-action window is the code's (tex comment: attack_operation.py / mtd_operation.py).
fix_text: "... exploits or brute-forces \citep{tay2024code}, and sends it back to scanning the same host's ports \citep{brown2023}"

claim: A service-layer deployment sends the attacker back to scanning the same host's ports
quote: Service and Operating System Diversity, and Port Shuffle all change the services on the host. This would either change the ports that the services are run on or change the service itself, changing the vulnerabilities. This would block the attacker from compromising the vulnerability and force them to re-perform a port scan to understand the new service or the service location.
issue: 'force them to re-perform a port scan'; 'the same host' is implicit in Brown (the services change on that host). Port shuffle, service and OS diversity are Brown's service class, matching Table 2.3's service layer.

claim: (uncited neighbour) A user shuffle disrupts only brute force, and sends the attacker to exploit instead
quote: When User Shuffle is performed, the users on the host change. This would only block the attack if the attacker was performing a credential stuffing attack as the users are shuffled, forcing them to look for vulnerabilities on the host.
issue: Brown: user shuffle blocks only 'a credential stuffing attack', forcing the attacker to look for vulnerabilities. The sentence says brute force. This is the code after Marc's D-07 ruling (2026-07-29: brute force is the one credential action with an interruptible window), so it is true of the code, but in a Brown-cited paragraph a reader who checks Brown sees 'credential stuffing'.
fix_text: optional: "A user shuffle disrupts only brute force, the one credential attack with time to disrupt, and ..."

claim: Year 2023
quote: This paper proposes an evaluation framework named MTDSim, which is a simulation-based tool to evaluate the effectiveness of combinations of MTD techniques against practical and realistic attack scenarios.
issue: EnCyCriS 2023.

claim: Property 1, campaign persistence: has it
quote: the attacker agent will move on after trying to exploit for 10 times without being able to compromise the host currently selected. However, when the attacker is conducting a targeted attack (i.e., scenario 2), the attacker is set to never give up on the target node.
locator: p. 7 printed (PDF p. 7), Sec. V-C; Sec. V-A
issue: Multi-stage procedure always followed, never giving up on the target node. 'Over an extended period' is not addressed by Brown; the mark is the dissertation's judgement on Brown's facts.

claim: Property 2, objective-specific behaviour: does not have it
quote: MTDSim looks to address this by implementing two attack scenarios with the same capabilities but with different goals in identical networks
issue: Same capabilities, different goals; only host choice differs between scenarios.

claim: Property 3, choice of attack strategy: in part
quote: The attacker will first attempt to perform a credential ... using user account information from previously compromised hosts. Next, a service from the scanning will be selected for exploitation. The vulnerabilities from all the services scanned will be put into a priority stack based on their return on attack (RoA) [13]. ... If the attack fails, they will then commence a brute force attack. If all attack options fail, they will then choose another host to exploit.
issue: Three routes in a fixed order.

claim: Property 4, adaptivity: in part
quote: IP Shuffle and Host Topology Shuffle change the location of the host by changing the IP or the host itself. This would result in the attacker’s connection to the host being terminated or timed out. As they would be uncertain of the status of the hosts, they would be forced to re-perform the host discovery phase to find new paths to the hosts.
issue: One fixed response per disruption class.

claim: Property 5, detection avoidance: does not have it
quote: This encompasses performing a scan on the network to discover all exposed hosts.
issue: Active network scan; Brown never mentions detection, an IDS or stealth (only 'remain undetected' in the introduction, about defenders).

claim: Property 6, cost-benefit reasoning: does not have it
quote: The vulnerabilities from all the services scanned will be put into a priority stack based on their return on attack (RoA) [13].
issue: Brown's RoA priority stack is a benefit-for-cost ordering, but of vulnerabilities within one technique (exploit), not a choice among techniques; Fig. 3's note also has host choice minimise time. 'None' is defensible under Table 3.2's 'chooses each technique', but an examiner who knows Brown could argue 'in part' under the partial rule ('a fixed rule in its place'), as round 51 once scored it. Judgement, not a citation defect.

claim: Property 7, learning: does not have it
quote: it is assumed that the attacker will instantly recognize that it has been previously compromised and regains control of the host.
issue: Brown's attacker remembers compromised hosts, not MTD patterns.

claim: Property 8, deployment-strategy awareness: does not have it
quote: All attacker agents in the simulation will always follow the attack procedure (as shown in Figure 3) to decide their next move.
issue: Nothing in Brown's attacker reads the defence schedule.
